# dmrconfig

**Command-line DMR codeplug tool — the text-file approach to the same job**

- **Version recorded:** 1.1+git20230126
- **Categories:** `dmr`, `radio-programming`, `station`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/sergev/dmrconfig>

## What it does

Reads a DMR radio's codeplug into a plain text configuration file, and writes an edited text file back to the radio. No GUI and no intermediate database — the codeplug is a file you edit with an editor.

## Why you would want it

It is the version-controllable answer to codeplug management. A text codeplug can live in git, diff between revisions, and be generated by a script from a contact list, none of which a binary blob or a GUI database supports. It is an alternative to qdmr rather than a companion: qdmr is better if you want to see the radio's structure, dmrconfig is better if you want to treat the codeplug as source.

## Before it will work

A radio in the right mode and access to its USB device. See the `dmr-radio` hardware class, and read its note about the permissions this package's own udev rule sets.

## How it installs

- apt: `dmrconfig`

## Known problems

Its shipped udev rule sets `MODE="666"` on the matching USB devices — world-readable and world-writable, by any user on the machine, with no group involved. qdmr's rule for the same identifiers uses `MODE="660", GROUP="dialout"`. Both are quoted verbatim in the `dmr-radio` class; the difference matters on a shared machine and matters more because one of the two identifiers is the generic STM32 bootloader, which is not specific to a radio at all.
The project name is one character from qdmr's command-line program `dmrconf`, and they are unrelated packages from different upstreams.

## Keeping it current

- probe: apt policy
